list.listitem: The most common presenting symptom of bladder tumor is painless hematuria. C
Cystoscopy and transurethral resection of the tumor are the best procedures for diagnosis and pathologic staging. B
The natural history of nonmuscle invasive bladder tumors is that of disease recurrence and progression to higher grade and stage. B
The standard therapy for nonmuscle invasive bladder tumor is transurethral resection and adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy or immunotherapy to prevent or delay the recurrence and progression. B

The best treatment for muscle-invasive tumors is radical cystectomy. Bladder-sparing surgery together with neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation is a reasonable alternative to radical cystectomy. B
The EORTC risk scores can determine prognosis (). B

background.definition: Bladder tumor is a malignant tumor within the bladder. It usually originates from the urothelial cells lining the bladder.

list.listitem: Estimated number of new cases of bladder tumor in the United States in 2007 was 67,160.

Although bladder tumor incidence is significantly higher in whites than in African Americans, the mortality rates are nearly the same, in large part because of the later stage at diagnosis among African Americans.
Bladder tumor is a very expensive disease to treat, with an estimated Medicare expenditure of US$96,000 to US$187,000 per patient in the United States from diagnosis to death (2001 values).
This is due to the long-term survival associated with nonmuscle-invasive disease combined with lifelong surveillance.
Bladder tumor is the fourth most common type of cancer in men and ninth most common in women in the United States.
It is currently the eighth leading cause of cancer death in men, with an estimated 13,750 deaths attributed to bladder cancer annually.
Cigarette smoking
Aniline dyes (2-naphthylamine, 4-aminobiphenyl, 4-nitrobiphenyl)
Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide

Patients taking pioglitazone for diabetes mellitus may be at increased risk for bladder cancer (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.09-1.39, NNH = 20,903/year)although other studies have not found an association.
Acrolein
Schistosomiasis
Pelvic irradiation
Chronic irritation and infection
Risk groups include workers in the following industries: printing, iron and aluminum processing, industrial painting, gas and tar manufacturing
Risk is also higher in patients who have undergone thymectomy.
As with all cancers, bladder tumor is associated with oxidative DNA genetic changes in the host cells, leading to abnormal and potentially uncontrolled growth.

Almost all bladder tumors are of epithelial origin. Among these urothelial tumors, more than 90% are transitional-cell carcinomas. However, up to 5% of bladder tumors are of squamous cell origin, and 2% are adenocarcinomas. Nonurothelial primary bladder tumors are extremely rare and may include small-cell carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, primary lymphoma, and sarcoma.

At diagnosis, bladder tumor is classified into 2 groups according to the invasiveness of the muscle wall of the bladder. Most patients (~75%-85%) present with nonmuscle invasive disease and have a long survival and high rate of recurrence and progression. Since tumor relapse rate increases with nuclear grade, nonmuscle-invasive bladder tumor is categorized as low- and high-grade tumors. The other group is termed "muscle-invasive" tumors.
The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends against routine screening for bladder tumor in adults. They did not review the evidence regarding screening in high-risk groups. B

Screening tests such as microscopic urinalysis, urine dipstick, and urine cytology, or such new tests as bladder tumor antigen (BTA) or nuclear matrix protein (NMP22) immunoassay can detect bladder cancers that are clinically unapparent. However, because of the low prevalence of bladder tumor, the positive predictive value of these tests is low. C
To reduce the risk of bladder tumor, patients should be advised to quit smoking, eat less animal fat, and eat more fruit and vegetables. B
Urinalysis is very sensitive in detecting the presence of hematuria but is nonspecific for bladder tumor. C
Urinary cytology has poor sensitivity (58%) but high specificity for malignancy; abnormal results may indicate urothelial tumor anywhere in the urinary tract. C
Cystoscopy and transurethral resection of the tumor are the recommended studies for patients with hematuria who are over age 40 years or have risk factors for bladder tumors. C

Most patients with bladder tumor present with painless hematuria; it can be continuous or intermittent and gross or microscopic. Gross painless hematuria in particular mandates further evaluation. In one study of 1000 consecutive patients evaluated for gross painless hematuria, 15% were found to have bladder tumor. Approximately 1.3% of patients with microscopic hematuria have an underlying bladder tumor (range 0.4%-6.5%).

Irritative voiding symptoms including frequency, urgency, and dysuria are particularly associated with carcinoma in situ (CIS). Nonmuscle-invasive tumors do not cause bladder pain and rarely present with bladder irritation, dysuria, and urgency. Pelvic pain and all the symptoms related to urinary tract obstruction are found in more advanced tumors. Indeed, the diagnosis of bladder tumor is a consideration in patients with irritative voiding symptoms in the absence of infection.

The physical examination of patients with bladder tumor is often unremarkable, especially in the case of nonmuscle-invasive disease. A bimanual examination at the time of transurethral resection of the bladder tumor may help with clinical staging, especially for patients with muscle-invasive disease.

Urinalysis is very sensitive in detecting the presence of hematuria but is not specific for bladder tumor. All patients with hematuria, particularly those without evidence of infections, stones, or other causative factors, should undergo cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.
For patients with microscopic hematuria, a systematic review of 30 studies with 24,366 patients found a prevalence of bladder cancer of 2% among patients presenting wih microscopic hematuria.
Lesions smaller than 0.5 cm that are flat and/or near the bladder neck can be easily missed with ultrasound.
Intravenous urography remains the best screen for upper-tract disease. The detection of hydronephrosis indicates poor prognosis because of invasive disease.

The primary contribution of CT is distinguishing tumors that are organ confined from those with extravesical extension. MRI is preferred over CT for local staging and is equivalent in the assessment of regional lymph nodes. A meta-analysis of 24 trials with 2928 patients confirmed the high specificity of MRI in staging lymph node metastases, but noted that MRI has low sensitivity.

Urinary cytology is an important adjunct in the diagnosis and surveillance of patients with urothelial carcinoma. Urinary cytology can be used to screen and evaluate patients at high risk for urothelial tumors (eg, those with hematuria or irritative voiding symptoms) and to monitor recurrence, progression, or response to treatment in patients with a known history of urothelial carcinoma. Sensitivity and positive predictive value of urinary cytology are particularly high in high-grade urothelial tumors as well as in cases of CIS in which sensitivities can exceed 90%. Positive results may indicate urothelial tumor anywhere in the urinary tract, not only in the bladder. The method has a lower sensitivity but a higher specificity than urine markers such as BTA stat test and NMP22.
Positive urine cytology in patients being followed up for bladder tumor without evidence of disease at the time of cystoscopy represents detection of subclinical disease that may subsequently recur.

Especially for low-grade tumors, urine cytology is of limited value because of low sensitivity. For that reason, many new urine-based tests, such as BTA stat, NMP22, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) have been developed.
Cystoscopy and transurethral resection of the tumor are the most reliable procedure for diagnosis and pathologic staging of the bladder tumor.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis examining the role of possible biomarkers as an alternative to cystoscopy demonstrated that these are of low accuracy in low stage and low grade tumours. In contrast, epigenetic profiling in patients presenting with hematuria appears promising in its high negative predictive value which may enable less invasive investigation of patients at low risk.

CxBladder is a series of tests based on 5 biomarkers to risk stratify patients presenting with hematuria. In a prospective validation study of 548 patients with hematuria, it was 90% sensitive and 96% specific for detection of clinically important tumors (LR+ 22, LR- 0.10).

BTA stat test is a qualitative, FDA-approved immunoassay. The assay detects bladder tumor associated antigen human complement factor H or a closely related protein. It is a rapid (about 5 min) point-of-care test that is generally easy to perform and interpret. The sensitivity and specificity of this test are 78% and 74%, respectively. Although the sensitivity of the BTA stat test is higher than that of cytology, specificity is much lower. In addition, benign inflammatory conditions may give false-positive results in over 25% of cases.

The NMP22 test is a quantitative, FDA-approved test. It is thought to detect the nuclear mitotic apparatus protein, which is present in the interphase nucleus and associated with the mitotic spindle during cell division. The sensitivity and specificity of this test are 50% and 82.8%, respectively.
Patients with bladder tumor history and a false-positive BTA stat test or NMP22 should be followed up more closely, because false positivity could correspond to an early event.

FISH is an assay intended to detect aneuploidy for chromosomes 3, 7, and 17 and loss of the 9p21 locus via FISH. In a multicenter, blinded, prospective trial, FISH assay was shown to have sensitivity at least equivalent to that of the BTA stat test and superior to cytology for the detection of recurrent urothelial carcinoma of the bladder. Its specificity approaches that of cytology, and its negative predictive value is better. It may also provide a much earlier diagnosis of cancer by identifying cases with no visible tumor that are at an earlier stage in the process. FISH has a higher specificity than other noninvasive urine markers, because it is not influenced by leukocytes or erythrocytes.

The EORTC clinical prediction rule for predicting recurrence and progression in patients with nonmuscle-invasive tumor is shown in and is also available online (http://www.eortc.be/tools/bladdercalculator). This estimates the probability of recurrence and progression over a period of 1 to 5 years based on a patients' clinical and pathological tumor characteristics at the time of surgery.

A second nomogram has been developed that predicts the probability of bladder tumor recurrence after radical cystectomy. It uses the following parameters: age, pathological stage, pathological lymph node status, lymphovascular invasion, presence of CIS, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and adjuvant radiation therapy.
For evaluation of hematuria, please see chapter on that topic and its algorithm. Patients with persistent hematuria and no evidence of infection or stones require cystoscopy and upper tract imaging.

Risk of recurrence and progression can be determined from .
The standard therapy for nonmuscle-invasive bladder tumor is transurethral resection and adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy or immunotherapy.B
The standard therapy for muscle-invasive bladder tumor is radical cystectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy. B
Patients with metastatic bladder tumors are usually treated with systemic chemotherapy. B

Intravesical drug instillations are used only for nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) after transurethral tumor resection. The goals of intravesical chemotherapy or immunotherapy are to eradicate existing disease, prevent tumor recurrence, and prevent tumor progression. A meta-analysis of 7 studies with 1373 patients suggests a lower recurrence rate with a combination of intravesical chemotherapy and BCG compared to BCG therapy alone.

The 2006 European Association of Urology (EAU) guidelines on nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer provide recommendations for adjuvant treatment after complete transurethral resection (TUR) of all papillary tumors. One immediate instillation after TUR reduces the recurrence rate and is recommended in all patients with papillary tumors, except in the case of a perforated bladder.

In a study of 113 BCG naive patients with NMIBC compared pirarubicin instilled once post-operatively with post-operatively plus 8 weekly instillations and found a higher likelihood of recurrece free survival in the latter group (85% vs 64%, NNT = 5, p = 0.004).
A trial by the Southwest Oncology Group of intravesical gemcitabine versus saline in low grade NMIBC following resection demonstrated a significant reduction in recurrence with gemcitabine.
An updated Cochrane review of intravesical therapy comparing gemcitabine with either mitomycin C or BCG found possible benefit from gemcitabine but with low level confidence in the overall results.

The need for further intravesical therapies and the choice of drug depend on the prognostic risk factors. The most important factors for recurrence are the number of tumors, their size, and the prior recurrence rate. The most important prognostic factors for progression are the T category, grade, and the presence of CIS, factors that represent the biological aggressiveness of the disease (see ).

See for recommended treatment based on risk status. In patients who are at low risk of both recurrence and progression, no further intravesical treatment is recommended. In patients who are at high risk of progression, BCG with 1 to 3 year of BCG maintenance is recommended.

In the remaining, so-called intermediate-risk patients, some form of adjuvant intravesical treatment is necessary. Meta-analyses have shown that both chemotherapy and BCG reduce the recurrence rate. Intravesical chemotherapy has not been shown to reduce the rate of progression to muscle-invasive disease, whereas BCG, which is more toxic, reduces the risk of progression when maintenance (at least 1 year) is given. The EAU guidelines recommend either BCG with 1 to 3 years of maintenance or a maximum of 1 year of chemotherapy.
Patients with CIS of the bladder also should be treated with BCG.

A systematic review of 5 poor quality clinical trials with 1111 patients found that BCG was more effective than epirubicin for patients with Ta and T1 stage bladder cancer at preventing recurrence, but there was no difference in mortality. BCG was associated with more adverse treatment effects.

A trial randomized 270 patients with newly diagnosed non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer to selenium, vitamin E, both or neither in a double-blind double-dummy fashion. After 5.5 years, there was no benefit or harm from selenium. However, those receiving vitamin E had a significantly decrease in the recurrence free interval (i.e. greater likelihood of recurrence) with hazard ratio of 1.46 (95% CI 1.02 - 2.09).
For patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, avelumab prolonged overall 1 year survival (71.3% vs 58.4%, p = 0.001, NNT = 6).
In a single-arm trial, 99 patients with unresectable or metastatic urothelial carcinoma who were given the tyrosine kinase inhibitor erdafitinib had a 40% response rate.

A phase 3 trial randomized 266 patients with advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma to erdafitinib or chemotherapy. After a median of 16 months follow-up, overall survival was significantly longer with erdafitinib (12.1 vs 7.8 months, p = .0005). Treatment relatived fatal events were also less common with erdafitinib (0.7% vs 5.4%).

Enfortumab vedotin is a monoclonal antibody against nectin-4, a cell adhesion molecule found in urothelial carcinomas. In an RCT of 608 patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, overall survival was significantly longer in the treatment group (12.9 vs 9.0 months, p = 0.001). The drug was well tolerated.

A further study combined enfortumab vedotin with pembrolizumab (checkpoint inhibitor PDL1 immunotherapy) comparing them against standard of care platinum/gemcitabine chemotherapy in locally advanced or metastatic disease. A total of 886 patients were included and there was both progression-free and overall survival advantage for the experimental group (median survival 31.5 versus 16.1 months).
Saticuzumab is a monoclonal antibody being evaluated for treatment of bladder cancer, but overall survival was lower than with enfortumab vedotin or erdafitinib.

A trial randomized 608 patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma to nivolumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin or gemcitabinre-cisplatin alone. Overall survival was longer with combination therapy (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.96); median survival was 21.7 months compared with 18.9 months.

Nonmuscle-invasive tumors: TUR is essential for the true staging and initial treatment of nonmuscle-invasive tumor. Without the presence of muscle, it is impossible to stage the tumor as Ta, T1, or T2. A re-TUR should be performed when the initial resection has been incomplete or the specimen contains no muscle tissue. Re-TUR also should be performed when TaT1, high-grade tumor has been detected at the initial TUR. It should be performed within 2 to 6 weeks after the first TUR.

For surgical therapy of muscle-invasive tumors, radical cystectomy plus pelvic lymphadenectomy is the standard treatment in most countries. A Cochrane review found that pre-operative radiotherapy followed by radical cystectomy was more effective than radical radiotherapy with salvage cystectomy.
Bladder-sparing surgery together with neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation is a reasonable alternative to radical cystectomy.
There are only limited data regarding different approaches to the use of intestinal segments to replace bladder function, with no clear evidence to choose one approach over another.
NICE guidance recommends that multidisciplinary teams plan the management with specialist surgeons undertaking operations. This is especially the case for laparoscopic cystectomy.

Innovation in surgical options prompted the trial of robot assisted radical cystectomy versus open radical cystectomy (the RAZOR trial). The robot surgery was non-inferior and worthy of further research.
A small series (n=72) comparing robot versus open radical cystectomy found no benefit in health related quality of life in the robot group.

A meta-analysis of en-bloc versus conventional transurethral resection for bladder cancer concluded that there was a survival benefit to en-bloc resection, but this may be influenced by unmeasured and unadjusted confounding and selection bias; randomized trials are lacking.

External beam radiation therapy has two indications: (1) patients who are candidates for total cystectomy but who are offered primary radiotherapy for bladder preservation, with salvage cystectomy in case of persistent disease, and (2) patients in whom total cystectomy is not a therapeutic option because of either locally advanced disease or high age, major comorbidity, and/or decreased performance status.

A large randomised trial of post-operative nivolumab immunotherapy versus placebo in patients with PDL1>1% demonstrated significant benefit in disease free survival in the immunotheapy arm, which is promoting further research in this adjuvant setting.

The benefit of adjuvant immunotherapy is confirmed with a large randomised trial in high risk muscle invasvie disease with 702 patients randomised to one year of pembrolizumab or observation alone post resection. Disease free survival at 44 months follow-up was 29.6 months with pembrolizumab versus 14.2 months without pembrolizumab.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is intended for patients with muscle-invasive disease.

There is evidence that adding immunotherapy to neo-adjuvant chemotherapy will similarly improve outcomes. With peri-operative and adjuvant durvalumab in combination with platinum/gemcitabine as neoadjuvant therapy, a randomised trial of over 1000 patients showed improvement in 2 year survival from 75.2% to 82.2% with the additional of durvalumab.

Clinical studies of cisplatin-based chemotherapy combined with radiotherapy have demonstrated response rates of 60% to 80%, with 5-year survival rates of 50% to 60%. An individual patient level Cochrane meta-analysis of 491 patients from six studies found that cisplatin-based chemotherapy regimens reduced the risk of death (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI, 0.6-0.96). There were methodologic issues related to early termination of studies and crossovers within trials.An updated review with additional trials found benefit to platinum based combination chemotherapy for patients with invasive bladder cancer.

Gemcitabine plus carboplatin is an alternative for patients unable to tolerate cisplatin-based chemotherapy.A Cochrane review found 6 RCTs enrolling a total of 704 patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer. The trials were quite heterogeneous, and suggest possible benefit.
At least 1 year of maintenance therapy with intravesical chemotherapy and immunotherapy is needed.
Consider hospitalization in patients with gross hematuria if unstable or significantly anemic.

Although adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy and immunotherapy reduce the recurrence and progression after resection of the nonmuscle-invasive tumors, these tumors will recur in a high percentage of cases and progress to muscle-invasive tumor in a limited number of cases. B
Tumor recurrence is quite common, occurring in as many as 60% to 90% of patients treated with TUR alone. Progression is a much more threatening event, often resulting in the patient's death.

For Ta lesions, recurrence will occur in approximately 60% of cases, but progression is quite rare. Although most Ta tumors are of low grade, high-grade Ta lesions do occur and often demonstrate an aggressive natural history. These patients had a 39% rate of progression to muscle invasion, and 26% died of bladder tumor.
Stage T1 tumors usually demonstrate an unfavorable natural history. Overall, stage T1 tumors have a progression rate of 30%, but progression can occur in up to 50% of those that are of high grade.
Although the natural history of CIS can be quite variable, a significant number (54%) of these lesions will progress to muscle-invasive disease.
Muscle-invasive tumors can invade adjacent organs and metastasizes to distant organs (lung, liver, and bones) if left untreated.

Nonmuscle invasive bladder tumors: Although adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy and immunotherapy reduce the recurrence and progression after resection of nonmuscle-invasive tumors, these tumors will recur in a high percentage of cases and progress to muscle-invasive tumor in a limited number of cases.
Muscle-invasive bladder tumors: After cystectomy for muscle-invasive bladder tumor, up to 50% of patients may develop metastases.
The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio is not useful as a prognostic biomarker for patients with bladder cancer.
There is an association between CYP2E1 gene polymorphisms and progression of bladder cancer.

Recurrence is common following appropriate treatment for primary tumor, and there is a need for cystoscopic monitoring. Only patients with high-grade tumors (including CIS) at time of diagnosis should have regular upper tract surveillance. Upper tract imaging should be carried out for patients in all risk groups if hematuria occurs during follow-up and the bladder is tumor free.

Follow-up recommendations are shown below according to risk classification: Nonmuscle-invasive tumors (low risk): Cystoscopy at 3 months. If negative, follow-up cystoscopy is advised at 9 months and then yearly for 5 years. Nonmuscle-invasive tumors (high risk): Cystoscopy at 3 months. If negative, the follow-up cystoscopies should be repeated every 3 months for a period of 2 years, every 4 months in the third year, every 6 months thereafter until 5 years, and yearly thereafter. Nonmuscle-invasive tumors (intermediate risk): Recommend an "in-between" follow-up scheme adapted according to personal and subjective factors. Muscle-invasive bladder tumors: Follow-up of these patients after cystectomy and radiotherapy is recommended to detect local recurrence and distant metastases.

cell.label: Transurethral resection (TUR). One immediate (within 24 hours) intravesical instillation of chemotherapy (mitomycin-C/40 mg).
Assess risk status: low risk (TaG1, T1G1 ≤3 cm single tumor); high risk (T1G2 multiple tumor, TaG3 tumor, T1G3 tumor, CIS); intermediate risk (all other).
No adjuvant therapy. Follow-up with cystoscopy.
Consider re-TUR when TaT1, high grade tumor has been detected at the initial TUR.
Radical cystectomy or bladder-sparing surgery together with neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy.
